title: Don't make this mistake
summary: NH tells how his deadlift stalled at 485 lb for months because he slowly started bending over the bar more and pulling with a rounded lower back. He didn't notice until he saw his PR footage, then denied it out of ego. Going back to his old upright technique and intention got him an immediate 495x2 PR. His lesson: poor form is a choice, so film yourself and stay honest.
claims: The deadlift is essential for bodybuilders who want to develop the upper back and posterior chain
He had never been hurt deadlifting, which he credits to always driving with his legs and not his lower back
He stalled at 485 lb for months with erratic performance, and his lower back was occasionally sore, which he'd never had before
When the lift stalled he did a 'tonnage sacrifice', switching to other lower-body lifts for a while
Footage of his 485x5 PR showed a cat-back deadlift from rep one: hips shooting up, thoracic extension lost, all lower back
Seeing the bad footage, his ego made him rationalise it, and he even wrote a description saying the rounding was on purpose before deleting the video
If you feel the need to justify your form ahead of time, you already know it's wrong
Cause: one day he bent over the bar more, the lift felt harder, and he decided he needed more lower back, which snowballed as the weight went up
The form drift was already visible at 465 and 475 lb before the 485 plateau; he was his own plateau
The bad habit spread to his snatch-grip deadlift too
Back with his old upright technique less than a week later, the warm-ups flew up and he hit 495x2, an all-time PR, with 2 more reps left
After the 495 PR he did 4 sets with 425 lb that felt like nothing
Good form depends mostly on technique and intention, not weak muscles; his cue is grab the bar, pull the slack, stay vertical, not 'grip and rip'
He fixed his form with no corrective exercises, only a change of intention
Poor form is a choice: if you can do your warm-ups with good form, you can do your top sets with good form
Deadlifts aren't bad for your back; deadlifting with bad form is
No human benefits from a rounded lower back in the deadlift; very few can round the thoracic spine while keeping the lumbar neutral
People bend over more because the upright position is slower and harder off the floor; bending gives fake explosiveness at the cost of safety
Fixing form usually doesn't cost progress; the more neutral spine often carries over better
Film your lifts about once a month to check technique and be honest with yourself
Teenagers rushing to a 405 or 500 lb deadlift with no care for technique end up injured and blaming the lift
exercises: grab the bar, pull the slack, stay vertical, drive with the legs, neutral spine, no hips shooting up
builds the upper back and posterior chain safely
rounding the lower back under max loads risks injury
same upright intention; don't bend over
training_log: all-time PR, upright form, about 2 more reps left
